intro: European colonization changed who commissioned pictures and what they pictured. These examples span colonial genres and later regional practices, with very different reasons to make an image.
alt: A fibrous bark-paper picture, a gilded devotional painting, a colonial-style family scene and a bright market painting.

variants.name: amate
variants.look: The warm brown paper and its rough edge remain visible between brightly painted birds or plants.
variants.history: Bark paper has a long history in Mexico. In modern amate painting, Otomí makers of paper and Nahua painters are both central to the story of the medium.
variants.when: Study a painted sheet alongside information about the people who made the paper and the picture.
variants.why: A fibrous ground adds a visible texture beneath even the flattest painted color.

variants.name: Cuzco School
variants.look: A dark devotional image stands out against gilded decoration and a richly colored surface.
variants.history: Colonial painters in and around Cusco adapted European religious imagery and developed distinctive workshop practices, including painting richly decorated garments.
variants.when: Study the meeting of local techniques and imported religious imagery in a surviving painting.
variants.why: Attention to the painted surface reveals choices that a broad label like colonial painting can conceal.

variants.name: casta painting
variants.look: A carefully staged family occupies a domestic scene with small details of clothing and objects.
variants.history: Many eighteenth-century paintings from New Spain classified people of mixed ancestry within a colonial racial hierarchy. Series commonly used family groupings and inscriptions.
variants.when: Study how picture placement and domestic detail were used to manufacture categories and hierarchy.
variants.why: A scene that looks ordinary at first can give a constructed political classification the appearance of common sense.

source.label: Los Angeles County Museum of Art

variants.name: Haitian painting
variants.look: Small repeated forms, bright color and high viewpoints draw the eye through an imagined market.
variants.history: Haitian painting encompasses many practices. Artists associated with Le Centre d'Art in twentieth-century Port-au-Prince helped make diverse Haitian approaches widely known.
variants.when: Start with a named painter's work when studying the arrangement of a crowded everyday scene.
variants.why: Repeated shapes can guide viewers across a large gathering while preserving differentiated encounters.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Mexican amate paper contemporary painting, brightly colored birds and flowers across a handmade brown bark sheet with a fibrous deckle edge; Cuzco School colonial Andean devotional image, gilded tracery and deep pigments in an ornate gallery frame; casta painting shown critically in a museum as a framed fictional colonial family group in a domestic setting, no racial labels or readable writing; Haitian popular painting fictional market garden, dense saturated flat color, repeated stepped trees and perspectives. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
